Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, [[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]], [[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $k[S_n]$ are indexed by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $\gamma$ a $p$-core, $w\in\mathbb N_0$ and $n=|\gamma|+pw$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$ with $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$ ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and let
$x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. The **hook of $x$** is the set
$$H(x):=\{(i,j')\in[\lambda]:j'\ge j\}\cup\{(i',j)\in[\lambda]:i'\ge i\},$$
the union of the boxes of $[\lambda]$ weakly to the right of $x$ in row $i$
and weakly below $x$ in column $j$; the box $x$ itself belongs to both parts
and is counted once. The **arm** $\operatorname{arm}(x)$ is the part in row
$i$ strictly to the right of $x$, so
$\operatorname{arm}(x)=\{(i,j'):j<j'\le\lambda_i\}$; the **leg**
$\operatorname{leg}(x)$ is the part in column $j$ strictly below $x$, so
$\operatorname{leg}(x)=\{(i',j):i<i'\le\lambda'_j\}$. The **arm length** is
$a(x):=\lambda_i-j$, the **leg length** is $\ell(x):=\lambda'_j-i$, and the
**hook length** is

$$h(x):=a(x)+\ell(x)+1=\lambda_i-j+\lambda'_j-i+1,$$

so that $H(x)$ has exactly $h(x)$ boxes. Here $\lambda'_j$ is the number of
rows of $[\lambda]$ of length at least $j$, so the boxes of column $j$ below
row $i$ are exactly the rows $i+1,\dots,\lambda'_j$ and the arm has
$\lambda_i-j$ boxes; the arm, the leg and the anchor $x$ are pairwise disjoint
and exhaust $H(x)$, which gives the count.

A box is removable in the sense of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] if and only if it is the
last box of its row and of its column, i.e. if and only if $h(x)=1$: a row
endpoint $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable exactly when no box lies immediately
below it, that is when $\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$, and then
$a(x)=\lambda_i-\lambda_i=0$ and $\ell(x)=\lambda'_{\lambda_i}-i=0$; conversely
$h(x)=1$ forces $a(x)=\ell(x)=0$, so $x$ ends both its row and its column. The
empty partition has no boxes.

Finally $P(\lambda):=\prod_{x\in[\lambda]}h(x)$ denotes the **hook product**
of $\lambda$, the empty product $P(\varnothing)=1$ being part of the
convention. This fixes the off-by-one convention used by the whole page: the
anchor box contributes $1$, the arm contributes $\lambda_i-j$ and the leg
contributes $\lambda'_j-i$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. Let $H(x)$ be the hook of $x$,
with arm length $a(x)=\lambda_i-j$, leg length $\ell(x)=\lambda'_j-i$ and hook
length $h(x)=a(x)+\ell(x)+1$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); its two endpoints are the last node
$(i,\lambda_i)$ of its arm and the last node $(\lambda'_j,j)$ of its leg. Let
$\xi(x)$ be the unique edge-connected set of nodes of $[\lambda]$ with
endpoints $(i,\lambda_i)$ and $(\lambda'_j,j)$ that lies in the rim of
$[\lambda]$, i.e. consists of nodes $(p,q)$ with $(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Then:

1. $\xi(x)$ is a removable border strip of $\lambda$ of size $h(x)$ and height
   $\ell(x)$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
   $[\lambda]\setminus\xi(x)$ is a Young diagram, so $\lambda\setminus\xi(x)$ is
   a partition of $n-h(x)$;
2. every removable border strip of $\lambda$ equals $\xi(x)$ for exactly one
   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes
   of $[\lambda]$ onto the removable border strips of $\lambda$.

Consequently the sizes of the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly
the hook lengths of $\lambda$, the height of $\xi(x)$ is the leg length
$\ell(x)$, and $x$ is removable as a node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) if and only if $\xi(x)$
has size $1$. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: The partition $(5)$. Its hook-length diagram is the single row $5,4,3,2,1$, so by [F1] the unique hook of length $3$ is $H_{1,3}(5)$, a horizontal rim hook of size $3$ spanning the nodes $(1,3),(1,4),(1,5)$ whose removal leaves the partition $(2)$; hence $(5)$ has exactly one removable $3$-hook. Its $\beta$-set is $X_\lambda=\{b_1\}=\{5\}$, a single bead on runner $2$ at row $1$; top-packing slides it to row $0$, so $X^{(3)}=\{2\}$ and $C_3((5))=P(\{2\})=(2)$, a $3$-core since $2<3$ and $(2)$ has hook lengths $2,1$.

The partition $(4,1)$. Its hook-length diagram is $5,3,2,1$ in the first row and $1$ in the second, so by [F1] the unique hook of length $3$ is $H_{1,2}(4,1)$, whose rim hook is the horizontal strip $(1,2),(1,3),(1,4)$ with complement $(1,1)$; hence $(4,1)$ also has exactly one removable $3$-hook. Its $\beta$-set is $X_\mu=\{b_1,b_2\}=\{5,1\}$, with $5$ on runner $2$ at row $1$ and $1$ on runner $1$ at row $0$; top-packing slides the bead $5$ to the position $2$, so $X^{(3)}=\{2,1\}$ and $C_3((4,1))=P(\{2,1\})=(1,1)$, a $3$-core since $(1,1)$ has hook lengths $2,1$.

The two partitions therefore have the same number (one) of removable $3$-hooks, but their $3$-cores are the distinct partitions $(2)$ and $(1,1)$ of size $2$; by [F3] the Specht modules $S^{(5)}_k$ and $S^{(4,1)}_k$ lie in different blocks of $k[S_5]$ for every splitting field $k$ of characteristic $3$. The top-packed abacus test of [F2] distinguishes the two configurations (one bead on runner $2$ versus beads on runners $2$ and $1$), while the local removable-hook count does not, so no such count can replace the core test. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

Both partitions have $3$-weight $1$, so even the weight may agree while the blocks differ; the invariant that separates them is the runner distribution of the beads, not the number of removable hooks.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n,0^{d-n})\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the length-$d$ composition with $n$ entries equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.

2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional
commutative $F$-algebra, and the identity $1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents of $A$: each $e_i$ is a
nonzero idempotent of $Z(A)$ that is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal
idempotents of $Z(A)$. No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed and no choice
principle is used.

Let $A$ be a unital ring ([[def-ring]]), with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A: za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$. Suppose that
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k=f_1+\cdots+f_\ell$$
where $\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$ and $\{f_1,\dots,f_\ell\}$ are finite families of
pairwise orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ that are primitive among central
idempotents: each is nonzero and admits no decomposition as a sum of two nonzero
orthogonal central idempotents (zero parts are omitted). Then $k=\ell$ and there
is a bijection $\sigma$ of the index sets with $e_i=f_{\sigma(i)}$ for all $i$;
in particular the decomposition of $1$ into primitive central idempotents is
unique up to order. No choice principle is used, the families being finite.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]), let $n\ge0$ and $d\ge n$, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl modules of $S_F(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then for partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S_F(d,n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently, for finite $e$, the blocks of $S_F(d,n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. For $e=\infty$ we set $C_\infty(\lambda):=\lambda$; the algebra is semisimple and its blocks are indexed by the partitions of $n$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not

([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],

([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).

by [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]:
that theorem proves the nonzero Murphy quotient criterion in $e$-restricted
labels, and conjugation makes these precisely $e$-regular labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

derivations.claim: Central idempotents of $H$ from blocks of $S$. For a block $C$ of $S$ with primitive central idempotent $\epsilon_C$ put $\tilde\epsilon_C:=\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Ce\in H$. This element is a central idempotent of $H$: it is idempotent because $\epsilon_C$ is, and for $x=ese\in H$ centrality of $\epsilon_C$ gives $x\tilde\epsilon_C=es\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Cse=\tilde\epsilon_Cx$; it is nonzero because it acts as the identity on the nonzero module $W^{\lambda}_Fe=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ for any $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}_F\in C$, namely $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\tilde\epsilon_C=W^{\lambda}_Fe\epsilon_Ce=W^{\lambda}_F\epsilon_Ce=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Moreover $\tilde\epsilon_C\tilde\epsilon_{C'}=e\epsilon_C\epsilon_{C'}e=0$ for $C\ne C'$ and $\sum_C\tilde\epsilon_C=e\sum_C\epsilon_Ce=e^2=1_H$.

Number of Hecke blocks is at least the number of q-Schur blocks. Decompose each nonzero central idempotent $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 into primitive central idempotents of $H$ using the unique decomposition of $1_H$: every primitive central idempotent $\delta_D$ of $H$ with $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C=\delta_D$ belongs to exactly one $\tilde\epsilon_C$, because $\delta_D=\delta_D\cdot1_H=\sum_C\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C$ and pairwise orthogonality of the $\delta_D$ forces $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C\in\{0,\delta_D\}$. Since each $\tilde\epsilon_C\ne0$ has at least one such $\delta_D$, the blocks $D$ of $H$ are partitioned into nonempty supports over the blocks $C$ of $S$, and therefore $\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}$.

A bijection of block sets, and the core criterion. By steps 2.1 and 1.2 the two block counts are equal, so each $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 has exactly one primitive summand and the map $C\mapsto\tilde\epsilon_C$ is a bijection from the blocks of $S$ onto the blocks of $H$. Since $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\lambda}_Fe$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\mu}_Fe$, the modules $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}$ lie in the same Hecke block if and only if $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same q-Schur block: indeed the block of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the image under the bijection of the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$. By the block theorem [F4] the latter holds if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, which proves the q-Schur-normalised statement.

Ordinary normalisation and semisimplicity. By [F5], $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block exactly when $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$ do. Step 3.1 makes this equivalent to $C_e(\lambda')=C_e(\mu')$, and the identity $C_e(\nu')=C_e(\nu)'$ makes it equivalent to $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$. This identity follows by conjugating every removable border strip in a core-removal sequence; the terminal core also conjugates, by independence of removal order. For $e=\infty$, $S$ is semisimple by [F4]. Its corner $eSe$ is semisimple: by [[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]], in the Wedderburn decomposition of $S$, each idempotent selects a subspace in each matrix factor, and its corner is a product of matrix algebras over the same division rings. Thus $H\cong eSe$ is semisimple; the block bijection separates the partition labels. This proves all assertions.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$

with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$

symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of

base change.

=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, [[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]], [[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $k[S_n]$ are indexed by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $\gamma$ a $p$-core, $w\in\mathbb N_0$ and $n=|\gamma|+pw$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$ with $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$ ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $n\ge0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $\Omega_\lambda$ be the finite set
of $\lambda$-tabloids; for a $\lambda$-tableau $t$ write $\{t\}$ for its
tabloid ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). The
**integral tabloid module** is the free abelian group on $\Omega_\lambda$,

$$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\mathbb Z^{(\Omega_\lambda)} =\Bigl\{\sum_{T\in\Omega_\lambda}a_T\,T:\ a_T\in\mathbb Z,\ \text{only finitely many }a_T\ne0\Bigr\},$$

with the tabloids as standard $\mathbb Z$-basis
([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). The left action of $S_n$ on
tabloids extends $\mathbb Z$-linearly to $M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so that
$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ is a $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-module. For every $\lambda$-tableau
$t$ put

$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma \in\mathbb Z[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\, \{\gamma\cdot t\}\in M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},$$

the **integral column polytabloid**; every coefficient lies in
$\{0,1,-1\}$ ([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]).
The **integral Specht lattice** is the $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-submodule

$$S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\text{the }\mathbb Z\text{-span of } \{\,e_s:\ s\text{ a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\,\}\subseteq M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}.$$

For a commutative ring $R$ let $M^\lambda_R:=R^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$ be the free
$R$-module on the tabloids and let $S^\lambda_R\subseteq M^\lambda_R$ be the
$R$-span of the polytabloids $\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)
\{\gamma\cdot t\}$, $t$ a $\lambda$-tableau. The **standard polytabloids** are
the $e_s$ with $s$ a standard $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).

This item records three facts. First, the standard polytabloids form a
$\mathbb Z$-basis of $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so the integral Specht lattice has
explicit finite rank. Second, for every commutative ring $R$ the canonical map
$R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\to R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}
M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\cong M^\lambda_R$ is injective onto $S^\lambda_R$: the
lattice is a direct summand of the free tabloid module and is compatible with
base change, including rings of prime characteristic. Third, for
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the module has rank one and is generated by the empty
polytabloid.

Fix a prime $p$, an integer $n\ge0$, and a **splitting $p$-modular system**
$(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$, so that $K$ and $k$ are splitting fields for
$S_n$ and its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). Write

$$M^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad S^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\subseteq M^\lambda_k$$

for the base change of the integral tabloid module and Specht lattice; the
inclusion is the injective polytabloid-span inclusion of
[[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]], and $S^\lambda_k$ has the
images of the standard polytabloids as $k$-basis. Let
$\beta_k:M^\lambda_k\times M^\lambda_k\to k$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form, the unique $k$-bilinear form with orthonormal tabloid basis
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]]); it is
symmetric, nondegenerate, and $S_n$-invariant.

For a $k$-subspace $V\subseteq M^\lambda_k$ put

$$V^{\perp}:=\{\,x\in M^\lambda_k:\beta_k(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\,\}.$$

The **form radical** of $S^\lambda_k$ is

$$R^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k\cap (S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},$$

and the **modular Specht quotient** (or James quotient) is

$$D^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda .$$

The quotient is a $k[S_n]$-module and may be zero. Its dimension is the
$p$-rank of the integral Gram matrix: if $G_\lambda$ is the Gram matrix of
$\beta$ in the standard-polytabloid basis and $\overline{G_\lambda}$ its
reduction modulo $p$, i.e. the matrix of $\beta_k$ in the standard basis of
$S^\lambda_k$, then

$$\dim_kD^\lambda=\operatorname{rank}_k\overline{G_\lambda} =\operatorname{rank}_k(G_\lambda\bmod p).$$

Everything is defined by scalar extension: $S^\lambda_k$ and $\beta_k$ are
determined by $\lambda$ and $k$, and no choice of lifts of elements of
$S^\lambda_k$ enters. $R^\lambda$ is a **form radical**, and is an
$S_n$-submodule; the identification of $R^\lambda$ with the module radical
$\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)=J(k[S_n])S^\lambda_k$
([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]) is a later consequence,
asserted only when $D^\lambda\ne0$. In particular no simplicity of
$D^\lambda$ is claimed here.

derivations.claim: The labels and their cores. The hook-length diagrams of the three partitions of $3$ are $3,2,1$ for $(3)$; $3,1$ in the first row and $1$ in the second for $(2,1)$; and $3,2,1$ vertically for $(1,1,1)$. In each case there is exactly one hook of length $3$ and removing its rim hook leaves the empty partition, so all three partitions have $3$-core $\varnothing$; conversely any partition of $3$ with core $\varnothing$ is one of these, since a partition whose core has size $3$ is its own core, and $\varnothing$ has size $0=3-3$. Dominance orders them as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$.

Compute the Weyl matrix directly. First work over $\mathbb F_3$ with lift $R=\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, $\hat q=1$, so the only nonzero hook valuation at rank three is $v([3]_1)=1$. The conjugate beta sequence of $(3)$ is $(3,2,1)$. Its hook pairs $(3,2)$ and $(3,1)$ give the balanced sequences $(5,0,1)$ and $(4,2,0)$, of sorted shapes $(1,1,1)$ with sign $-1$ and $(2,1)$ with sign $+1$, respectively. The other pair has coefficient zero. Thus its positive sum is $[W^{(2,1)}]-[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. For $(2,1)$, beta $(4,2,0)$ and its only nonzero pair $(3,1)$ give $(5,1,0)$, shape $(1,1,1)$ with sign $+1$, so its positive sum is $[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. The column shape has no row pair and zero positive sum, hence $W^{(1,1,1)}=L^{(1,1,1)}$. Positivity and $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ then show that $W^{(2,1)}(1)=L^{(1,1,1)}$ and every higher submodule is zero, giving $[W^{(2,1)}]=[L^{(2,1)}]+[L^{(1,1,1)}]$. Substitute into the first sum to get $[L^{(2,1)}]$; the same argument gives $[W^{(3)}]=[L^{(3)}]+[L^{(2,1)}]$. This proves exactly the displayed complete Weyl matrix. Scalar extension to any original field $F$ of characteristic three preserves the Weyl modules/forms and the composition series, since all Schur simple heads are absolutely simple by [F2].

Determine the specific corner images directly. The group row symmetrizer $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}w$ satisfies $x_{(3)}^2=6x_{(3)}$, so its rank-one Murphy form is zero in characteristic three. In the rank-one column cell the generator is $1$ and its square coefficient is $1$; the higher ideal contains $1+T_1$ and $1+T_2$ (the latter is a conjugate of the former), so this cell and its nonzero form quotient are the sign module. For the middle cell put $x=1+T_1$, $c_0=x$ and $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher row ideal. Its row symmetrizer satisfies $x_{(3)}=x+xT_2+xT_2T_1$, so $c_1T_1=-c_0-c_1$ while $c_0T_1=c_0$; and $T_2^2=1$ gives $c_0T_2=c_1$, $c_1T_2=c_0$. Thus its generator matrices are $M_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $M_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The independent cell products $x^2=2x$, $xT_2x=x_{(3)}-x\equiv-x$ and $xT_2^2x=2x$ give $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ over $F$. Its radical is the line $(1,-1)$; modulo it both generators act by $1$, so $D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,1)}$ is the nonzero trivial module. These two simple images are distinct since $1\ne-1$. The exact corner/form identity [F3] therefore kills precisely $L^{(3)}$ among the three labels. Projecting the Weyl matrix just proved gives all displayed Murphy Specht rows over the original $F$, without any general finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion.

Dipper-James rows and the direct group computation. Conjugating the partitions $(3)\leftrightarrow(1,1,1)$, $(2,1)\leftrightarrow(2,1)$ and applying the signed $\theta$-pullback to every Hecke module, the rows of step 3.1 become $[S^{(1,1,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]$, $[S^{(2,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]+[D^{(3)}]$ and $[S^{(3)}]=[D^{(3)}]$ in the $3$-regular labels, that is, the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ and columns $(3),(2,1)$. For the independent direct check, construct the tabloid module over $k$ using [F5]. Every middle-shape polytabloid is a difference $v_i-v_j$, and these span the two independent vectors $e_t,e_u$ displayed in [F5], so they are a basis of $S^{(2,1)}_k$. A one-row polytabloid is its unique tabloid, giving the trivial module; a one-column polytabloid is the nonzero alternating sum of all six distinct tabloids, giving the sign module. Put $w:=e_t+e_u=v_3-v_1+v_2-v_1=v_1+v_2+v_3$ in characteristic $3$: then $w\ne0$ spans a one-dimensional submodule, since $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$ gives $\sigma\cdot w=w$ for every $\sigma\in S_3$, so it realises the trivial module; and in the quotient, $(12)\cdot e_t+e_t=(v_3-v_2)+(v_3-v_1)=2v_3-v_1-v_2=3v_3-w\equiv0$ shows that $(12)$ acts by $-1$. All transpositions are conjugate and act on a one-dimensional quotient, so they all act by $-1$ and the quotient is sign. The orthonormal tabloid form has middle Gram matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ in $(e_t,e_u)$; its characteristic-three kernel is $k(e_t+e_u)=kw$. Thus the James quotient $D^{(2,1)}$ is precisely this sign quotient, while the row form has norm $1$ and $D^{(3)}$ is trivial. With $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F5], and the just-computed $D^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $D^{(2,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ (the complete list is [F4]), the direct rows of $S^{(3)},S^{(2,1)},S^{(1,1,1)}$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$, matching the matrix obtained from the Schur functor entry by entry.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a
$\beta$-set for $\lambda$, so that $P(X)=\lambda$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Write $H_i(\lambda)$ for
the set of hook lengths in row $i$ of $[\lambda]$: thus $h\in H_i(\lambda)$
means $h=h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ for some node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$, and
$H_i(\lambda)=\emptyset$ for $i>\ell(\lambda)$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]).

(i) For every $h\ge0$ and every $i\in[m]$, $h\in H_i(\lambda)$ if and only if
$h\le h_i$ and $h_i-h\notin X$. Equivalently, the hooks of $\lambda$
correspond bijectively to the **bead-gap pairs** $(b,g)$ with $b\in X$,
$g\notin X$ and $0\le g<b$; the hook $H_{i,j}(\lambda)$ corresponds to
$$(b,g)=\bigl(h_i,\;h_i-h_{i,j}(\lambda)\bigr),$$
and then $|H_{i,j}(\lambda)|=b-g$.

(ii) Fix a node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$ and let $(b,g)$ be its bead-gap pair as in
(i). Then
$$X':=(X\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$$
is again a $\beta$-set, now for the partition $\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}$
obtained from $\lambda$ by removing the removable border strip $R_{i,j}$ that
corresponds to the hook of $(i,j)$, of size $h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ and height
$\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]); in terms of parts, with
$b_0:=\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$,
$$\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}=\bigl(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{i-1},\,\lambda_{i+1}-1,\dots,\lambda_{i+b_0}-1,\,j-1,\,\lambda_{i+b_0+1},\dots\bigr),$$
so that $|\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}|=n-h_{i,j}(\lambda)$. Finally $X'$ is
obtained from the configuration $A_X$ by moving the bead from position $b$ to
the gap $g$.

(iii) In particular $e\mid h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ if and only if $b\equiv g\pmod e$,
that is, if and only if the bead $b$ and the gap $g$ lie on the same runner of
the $e$-abacus; then $g=b-e\cdot(h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e)$ and the move in (ii) is
the slide of the bead $b$ up $h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e$ rows on its own runner. A
hook of length $e$ in row $i$ of $\lambda$ exists if and only if $h_i\ge e$
and $h_i-e\notin X$; Thus $\lambda$ has a hook of length $e$ if and only if some bead of $X$ has a gap
in the position $e$ labels above it on its own runner.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-quotient
$Q_e(\lambda)=(\lambda^{(0)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)})$ and $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then there is a
bijection $f$ from the set of hooks of $\lambda$ of $e$-divisible length onto
the set of hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$, that is, onto
$\bigsqcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{\text{hooks of }\lambda^{(i)}\}$, such that
$$|H|=e\,|f(H)|\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q_e\bigl(\lambda\setminus H\bigr)=Q_e(\lambda)\setminus f(H),$$
where the right-hand side means that the hook $f(H)$ is removed from the single
component of $Q_e(\lambda)$ that contains it. On the $e$-abacus, $f$ is the
rescaling $b=b'e+i$, $g=g'e+i$ of a bead-gap pair $(b,g)$ lying on a common
runner $i$, followed by the bead-gap dictionary of the runner
([[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]]).

Here and in the quotient components, removing a hook means deleting its
corresponding rim border strip as in
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](ii), rather than its arm-and-leg
node set.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-core $C_e(\lambda)$ and
$e$-weight $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then
$$n=|\lambda|=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda),$$
so $w_e(\lambda)=(n-|C_e(\lambda)|)/e\in\mathbb N_0$. Equivalently every
sequence of removals of removable border strips of size $e$ from $\lambda$ down
to its $e$-core
([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]) has exactly
$w_e(\lambda)$ steps, and $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$ equals both the number
of hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$ and, by the bijection of
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]], the number of hooks of
$\lambda$ of length divisible by $e$.

Throughout the proof, $\lambda\setminus H$ means deletion of the rim strip
corresponding to the node hook $H$, as in
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]].

No choice principle is used.

$$\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}=\bigl(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{i-1},\,\lambda_{i+1}-1,\dots,\lambda_{i+b_0}-1,\,j-1,\,\lambda_{i+b_0+1},\dots\bigr),$$
so that $|\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}|=n-h_{i,j}(\lambda)$. Finally $X'$ is
obtained from the configuration $A_X$ by moving the bead from position $b$ to
the gap $g$.

(iii) In particular $e\mid h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ if and only if $b\equiv g\pmod e$,
that is, if and only if the bead $b$ and the gap $g$ lie on the same runner of
the $e$-abacus; then $g=b-e\cdot(h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e)$ and the move in (ii) is
the slide of the bead $b$ up $h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e$ rows on its own runner. A
hook of length $e$ in row $i$ of $\lambda$ exists if and only if $h_i\ge e$
and $h_i-e\notin X$; Thus $\lambda$ has a hook of length $e$ if and only if some bead of $X$ has a gap
in the position $e$ labels above it on its own runner.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. Let $H(x)$ be the hook of $x$,
with arm length $a(x)=\lambda_i-j$, leg length $\ell(x)=\lambda'_j-i$ and hook
length $h(x)=a(x)+\ell(x)+1$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); its two endpoints are the last node
$(i,\lambda_i)$ of its arm and the last node $(\lambda'_j,j)$ of its leg. Let
$\xi(x)$ be the unique edge-connected set of nodes of $[\lambda]$ with
endpoints $(i,\lambda_i)$ and $(\lambda'_j,j)$ that lies in the rim of
$[\lambda]$, i.e. consists of nodes $(p,q)$ with $(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Then:

1. $\xi(x)$ is a removable border strip of $\lambda$ of size $h(x)$ and height
   $\ell(x)$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
   $[\lambda]\setminus\xi(x)$ is a Young diagram, so $\lambda\setminus\xi(x)$ is
   a partition of $n-h(x)$;
2. every removable border strip of $\lambda$ equals $\xi(x)$ for exactly one
   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes
   of $[\lambda]$ onto the removable border strips of $\lambda$.

Consequently the sizes of the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly
the hook lengths of $\lambda$, the height of $\xi(x)$ is the leg length
$\ell(x)$, and $x$ is removable as a node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) if and only if $\xi(x)$
has size $1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-core $C_e(\lambda)$ and
$e$-weight $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then
$$n=|\lambda|=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda),$$
so $w_e(\lambda)=(n-|C_e(\lambda)|)/e\in\mathbb N_0$. Equivalently every
sequence of removals of removable border strips of size $e$ from $\lambda$ down
to its $e$-core
([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]) has exactly
$w_e(\lambda)$ steps, and $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$ equals both the number
of hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$ and, by the bijection of
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]], the number of hooks of
$\lambda$ of length divisible by $e$.

Throughout the proof, $\lambda\setminus H$ means deletion of the rim strip
corresponding to the node hook $H$, as in
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]].

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and let
$x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. The **hook of $x$** is the set
$$H(x):=\{(i,j')\in[\lambda]:j'\ge j\}\cup\{(i',j)\in[\lambda]:i'\ge i\},$$
the union of the boxes of $[\lambda]$ weakly to the right of $x$ in row $i$
and weakly below $x$ in column $j$; the box $x$ itself belongs to both parts
and is counted once. The **arm** $\operatorname{arm}(x)$ is the part in row
$i$ strictly to the right of $x$, so
$\operatorname{arm}(x)=\{(i,j'):j<j'\le\lambda_i\}$; the **leg**
$\operatorname{leg}(x)$ is the part in column $j$ strictly below $x$, so
$\operatorname{leg}(x)=\{(i',j):i<i'\le\lambda'_j\}$. The **arm length** is
$a(x):=\lambda_i-j$, the **leg length** is $\ell(x):=\lambda'_j-i$, and the
**hook length** is

$$h(x):=a(x)+\ell(x)+1=\lambda_i-j+\lambda'_j-i+1,$$

so that $H(x)$ has exactly $h(x)$ boxes. Here $\lambda'_j$ is the number of
rows of $[\lambda]$ of length at least $j$, so the boxes of column $j$ below
row $i$ are exactly the rows $i+1,\dots,\lambda'_j$ and the arm has
$\lambda_i-j$ boxes; the arm, the leg and the anchor $x$ are pairwise disjoint
and exhaust $H(x)$, which gives the count.

A box is removable in the sense of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] if and only if it is the
last box of its row and of its column, i.e. if and only if $h(x)=1$: a row
endpoint $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable exactly when no box lies immediately
below it, that is when $\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$, and then
$a(x)=\lambda_i-\lambda_i=0$ and $\ell(x)=\lambda'_{\lambda_i}-i=0$; conversely
$h(x)=1$ forces $a(x)=\ell(x)=0$, so $x$ ends both its row and its column. The
empty partition has no boxes.

Finally $P(\lambda):=\prod_{x\in[\lambda]}h(x)$ denotes the **hook product**
of $\lambda$, the empty product $P(\varnothing)=1$ being part of the
convention. This fixes the off-by-one convention used by the whole page: the
anchor box contributes $1$, the arm contributes $\lambda_i-j$ and the leg
contributes $\lambda'_j-i$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes
   of $[\lambda]$ onto the removable border strips of $\lambda$.

Consequently the sizes of the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly
the hook lengths of $\lambda$, the height of $\xi(x)$ is the leg length
$\ell(x)$, and $x$ is removable as a node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) if and only if $\xi(x)$

derivations.claim: Pad $\lambda$ with zeros to length $m$. By [F3], $h_i=\lambda_i+m-i$. Below $h_i$ there are exactly $m-i$ beads, hence $h_i-(m-i)=\lambda_i$ gaps. For a node $(i,j)$ put $g_j=h_i-h_{i,j}(\lambda)=m+j-1-\lambda'_j$. These values are distinct by [F1], satisfy $0\le g_j<h_i$, and are gaps: equality $g_j=h_x=\lambda_x+m-x$ would give $\lambda_x-j+\lambda'_j-x+1=0$. If $x\le\lambda'_j$, both differences are nonnegative; otherwise both are at most $-1$, since $\lambda_x<j$. Neither case gives zero. Thus the $\lambda_i$ numbers $g_j$ exhaust the gaps below $h_i$, including the empty set when $\lambda_i=0$.

Fix $(i,j)$ and put $r=\lambda'_j$ and $g=m+j-1-r$. The rim strip of [F4] has complement with rows $\mu_p=\lambda_p$ outside $i\le p\le r$, $\mu_p=\lambda_{p+1}-1$ for $i\le p<r$, and $\mu_r=j-1$: in row $p$ the strip occupies the rim nodes with column at least $j$, whose complement ends at $\max(j-1,\lambda_{p+1}-1)$. For $p<r$ one has $\lambda_{p+1}\ge j$, while $\lambda_{r+1}<j$. These formulas give the displayed partition in (ii), with trailing zeros deleted, and its size is $n-h_{i,j}(\lambda)$.

Consequently, for $h\ge0$, $h\in H_i(\lambda)$ exactly when $h\le h_i$ and $h_i-h\notin X$: at $h=0$ the latter fails because $h_i\in X$, and for $h>h_i$ its first inequality fails. For $1\le h\le h_i$ this is the gap correspondence in step 1.1. The bead $h_i$ determines $i$, and the distinct row hook lengths determine $j$, so $(i,j)\mapsto(h_i,g_j)$ is the asserted bijection with length $h_i-g_j$.

The new value $g$ is below $h_r$ because $h_r-g=\lambda_r-j+1\ge1$, and, if $r<m$, above $h_{r+1}$ because $g-h_{r+1}=j-\lambda_{r+1}\ge1$. Hence the decreasing list of $X'=(X\setminus\{h_i\})\cup\{g\}$ is $h_1,\ldots,h_{i-1},h_{i+1},\ldots,h_r,g,h_{r+1},\ldots,h_m$. Applying [F2] gives precisely the parts $\mu_p$ in step 1.2. Thus $P(X')=\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}$, and the abacus change is the relocation of the bead $h_i$ to $g$.

The length is $b-g$, so $e\mid h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ exactly when $b\equiv g\pmod e$. In that case the bead remains on its runner, moves up $h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e$ rows, and all runner bead counts are unchanged. Without this divisibility assumption the relocation may change runners. In row $i$ a hook of length $e$ exists exactly when $h_i\ge e$ and $h_i-e\notin X$, by step 2.1; existential quantification over $i$ gives the final bead criterion in (iii).
