Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-quotient
$Q_e(\lambda)=(\lambda^{(0)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)})$ and $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then there is a
bijection $f$ from the set of hooks of $\lambda$ of $e$-divisible length onto
the set of hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$, that is, onto
$\bigsqcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{\text{hooks of }\lambda^{(i)}\}$, such that
$$|H|=e\,|f(H)|\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q_e\bigl(\lambda\setminus H\bigr)=Q_e(\lambda)\setminus f(H),$$
where the right-hand side means that the hook $f(H)$ is removed from the single
component of $Q_e(\lambda)$ that contains it. On the $e$-abacus, $f$ is the
rescaling $b=b'e+i$, $g=g'e+i$ of a bead-gap pair $(b,g)$ lying on a common
runner $i$, followed by the bead-gap dictionary of the runner
([[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]]).

Here and in the quotient components, removing a hook means deleting its
corresponding rim border strip as in
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](ii), rather than its arm-and-leg
node set.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and let
$x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. The **hook of $x$** is the set
$$H(x):=\{(i,j')\in[\lambda]:j'\ge j\}\cup\{(i',j)\in[\lambda]:i'\ge i\},$$
the union of the boxes of $[\lambda]$ weakly to the right of $x$ in row $i$
and weakly below $x$ in column $j$; the box $x$ itself belongs to both parts
and is counted once. The **arm** $\operatorname{arm}(x)$ is the part in row
$i$ strictly to the right of $x$, so
$\operatorname{arm}(x)=\{(i,j'):j<j'\le\lambda_i\}$; the **leg**
$\operatorname{leg}(x)$ is the part in column $j$ strictly below $x$, so
$\operatorname{leg}(x)=\{(i',j):i<i'\le\lambda'_j\}$. The **arm length** is
$a(x):=\lambda_i-j$, the **leg length** is $\ell(x):=\lambda'_j-i$, and the
**hook length** is

$$h(x):=a(x)+\ell(x)+1=\lambda_i-j+\lambda'_j-i+1,$$

so that $H(x)$ has exactly $h(x)$ boxes. Here $\lambda'_j$ is the number of
rows of $[\lambda]$ of length at least $j$, so the boxes of column $j$ below
row $i$ are exactly the rows $i+1,\dots,\lambda'_j$ and the arm has
$\lambda_i-j$ boxes; the arm, the leg and the anchor $x$ are pairwise disjoint
and exhaust $H(x)$, which gives the count.

A box is removable in the sense of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] if and only if it is the
last box of its row and of its column, i.e. if and only if $h(x)=1$: a row
endpoint $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable exactly when no box lies immediately
below it, that is when $\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$, and then
$a(x)=\lambda_i-\lambda_i=0$ and $\ell(x)=\lambda'_{\lambda_i}-i=0$; conversely
$h(x)=1$ forces $a(x)=\ell(x)=0$, so $x$ ends both its row and its column. The
empty partition has no boxes.

Finally $P(\lambda):=\prod_{x\in[\lambda]}h(x)$ denotes the **hook product**
of $\lambda$, the empty product $P(\varnothing)=1$ being part of the
convention. This fixes the off-by-one convention used by the whole page: the
anchor box contributes $1$, the arm contributes $\lambda_i-j$ and the leg
contributes $\lambda'_j-i$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-quotient
$Q_e(\lambda)=(\lambda^{(0)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)})$ and $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then there is a
bijection $f$ from the set of hooks of $\lambda$ of $e$-divisible length onto
the set of hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$, that is, onto
$\bigsqcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{\text{hooks of }\lambda^{(i)}\}$, such that
$$|H|=e\,|f(H)|\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q_e\bigl(\lambda\setminus H\bigr)=Q_e(\lambda)\setminus f(H),$$
where the right-hand side means that the hook $f(H)$ is removed from the single
component of $Q_e(\lambda)$ that contains it. On the $e$-abacus, $f$ is the
rescaling $b=b'e+i$, $g=g'e+i$ of a bead-gap pair $(b,g)$ lying on a common
runner $i$, followed by the bead-gap dictionary of the runner
([[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]]).

Here and in the quotient components, removing a hook means deleting its
corresponding rim border strip as in
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](ii), rather than its arm-and-leg
node set.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: We first record the counting consequences of the quotient theorem. A hook of $\lambda$ has $e$-divisible length exactly when it is the preimage under the bijection $f$ of [F2] of a hook of $Q_e(\lambda)$, and the number of hooks of a partition equals its size by [F3]; hence the number of $e$-divisible hooks of $\lambda$ equals the total size $w_e(\lambda)=\sum_i|\lambda^{(i)}|$ of $Q_e(\lambda)$. In particular $Q_e(\lambda)$ has a hook if and only if $w_e(\lambda)>0$, and then some hook has size $1$ by [F3], so $\lambda$ has a hook of length $e$.

Base case: if $w_e(\lambda)=0$ then $Q_e(\lambda)$ has no hook by step 1.1, so $\lambda$ has no hook of $e$-divisible length, hence no hook of length $e$; by [F1] the terminal partition of the empty removal sequence is $\lambda$ itself, that is, $C_e(\lambda)=\lambda$, and the removal sequence has $0=w_e(\lambda)$ steps.

Induction step: let $w_e(\lambda)>0$. By step 1.1 there is a hook $H$ of $\lambda$ of length exactly $e$, a removable border strip of size $e$ by [F1]. By the removal identity of [F2], $$Q_e(\lambda\setminus H)=Q_e(\lambda)\setminus f(H),$$ and since $f(H)$ is a hook of a component of $Q_e(\lambda)$ of size $|H|/e=1$, the right-hand side is the multipartition obtained by deleting one box, so by [F3] its size is $w_e(\lambda)-1$. Moreover $C_e(\lambda\setminus H)=C_e(\lambda)$: a maximal sequence from $\lambda\setminus H$ is the tail of a maximal sequence from $\lambda$ beginning with $H$, and all maximal sequences from $\lambda$ end at $C_e(\lambda)$ by [F1].

By step 2.2 we may apply the induction hypothesis to $\lambda\setminus H$, whose weight is $w_e(\lambda)-1<w_e(\lambda)$: every maximal sequence of $e$-strip removals from $\lambda\setminus H$ has $w_e(\lambda)-1$ steps and $$|\lambda|-e=|\lambda\setminus H|=|C_e(\lambda\setminus H)|+e\,(w_e(\lambda)-1)=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda)-e,$$ so $|\lambda|=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda)$; and appending the single step $H$ shows that every maximal sequence from $\lambda$ has exactly $w_e(\lambda)$ steps, because $H$ was an arbitrary possible first $e$-hook removal and step 2.2 applies to every such first step.

The base case of step 2.1 and the induction step of steps 2.2 and 3.1 establish the size formula and the step count for every partition of finite weight, and the counting statement is step 1.1. This is all that was asserted.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, [[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]], [[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $k[S_n]$ are indexed by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $\gamma$ a $p$-core, $w\in\mathbb N_0$ and $n=|\gamma|+pw$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$ with $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$ ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Fix a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for a finite group $G$.
A **$p$-block idempotent** is a primitive central idempotent of $\mathcal O G$
or, after reduction, of $kG$.

If $e$ is such an idempotent, the corresponding **block** is the two-sided
ideal

$$B=\mathcal OGe\qquad\text{or}\qquad B=kGe.$$

The primitive central idempotents are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, so
the algebra splits as a direct product of its block summands.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$ with maximal ideal
$\mathfrak m\subseteq\mathcal O$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$S^\lambda_{\mathcal O}:=\mathcal O\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}, \qquad S^\lambda_K:=K\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}, \qquad S^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},$$
so that $S^\lambda_{\mathcal O}$ is a stable $\mathcal O[S_n]$-lattice in
$S^\lambda_K$ with reduction $S^\lambda_k$
([[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]],
[[def-og-lattice-and-reduction-modulo-the-maximal-ideal]]). For a
$p$-regular $\mu\vdash n$ let $D^\mu$ be the simple $k[S_n]$-module of
[[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]], and put
$$d_{\lambda\mu}:=[S^\lambda_k:D^\mu],$$
the multiplicity of $D^\mu$ in a composition series of $S^\lambda_k$. By the
definition of the decomposition map and its independence of the stable
lattice, $d_{\lambda\mu}$ is the decomposition number of the ordinary
irreducible $S^\lambda_K$ with respect to $D^\mu$
([[def-decomposition-map-from-ordinary-to-modular-grothendieck-groups]],
[[def-decomposition-numbers-and-decomposition-matrix]],
[[thm-decomposition-map-is-independent-of-the-stable-lattice]]). Then:

1. **Dominance bound.** $d_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless the $p$-regular partition
   $\mu$ dominates $\lambda$; equivalently, every composition factor of
   $S^\lambda_k$ is isomorphic to $D^\mu$ for some $p$-regular $\mu\unrhd
   \lambda$.
2. **Diagonal.** $d_{\lambda\lambda}=1$ for every $p$-regular
   $\lambda\vdash n$; that is, $D^\lambda$ occurs exactly once as a
   composition factor of $S^\lambda_k$.
3. **Lower unitriangular block.** List the $p$-regular partitions of $n$ in
   decreasing lexicographic order, put them first among the rows in that
   order, and use the same order for the columns. Then the square block
   $(d_{\lambda\mu})_{\lambda,\mu\ p\text{-regular}}$ is lower
   unitriangular: $d_{\lambda\mu}=0$ whenever $\mu$ is lexicographically
   strictly smaller than $\lambda$ (so its column occurs to the right of the
   diagonal), and $d_{\lambda\lambda}=1$.

The result is a constraint on the decomposition matrix, not a formula for
all of its entries. It uses no positivity of the modular form, no division
by a group order and no averaging, and it includes $n=0$ and
characteristic $2$.

If $D=(d_{\chi\varphi})$ is the decomposition matrix and
$C=(c_{\varphi\psi})$ is the Cartan matrix, then

$$C=D^{\mathsf T}D.$$

Equivalently,

$$c_{\varphi\psi}=\sum_\chi d_{\chi\varphi}d_{\chi\psi}.$$

For each irreducible Brauer character $\varphi$, let $S_\varphi$ be the
corresponding simple $kG$-module and let $P_\varphi\to S_\varphi$ be its
projective cover. The module $P_\varphi$ is an indecomposable projective
$kG$-module, and these exhaust the indecomposable projectives up to isomorphism.

Choose a projective $\mathcal O G$-lattice $\widehat P_\varphi$ whose reduction
is $P_\varphi$. Its ordinary character $\Phi_\varphi$ is called the
**projective indecomposable character** attached to $\varphi$. The existence of
such a projective lift and the independence of its ordinary character are
proved in [[thm-brauer-reciprocity]].

For irreducible Brauer characters $\varphi,\psi$, the multiplicity of
$S_\psi$ as a composition factor of $P_\varphi$ is denoted $c_{\varphi\psi}$.
The matrix $C=(c_{\varphi\psi})$ is the **Cartan matrix** of $G$ at $p$.

Over the splitting residue field $k$, the following are equivalent for a block $B=kGb$: its defect group is trivial; $B$ is a full matrix algebra over $k$; $B$ has a projective simple module. In that case there is exactly one simple module and it is projective.

Bookkeeping for the labels of $B$. Let $
u\vdash n$ be a $p$-regular partition with block $B(
u)=B$; by [F1] and [F2] this is equivalent to $C_p(
u)=C_p(\lambda)=\lambda$, and since $|
u|=n=|\lambda|$ this forces $
u=\lambda$. Hence the only $p$-regular label in $B$ is $\lambda$, and by [F2] the only simple module in $B$ is $D^{\lambda}$. For any Specht label $\mu$ in $B$, [F2] gives $C_p(\mu)=\lambda$ and $|\mu|=|\lambda|$, so $\mu=\lambda$ as well: the block has exactly one Specht row. Since $S^{\lambda}_k$ is indecomposable with head $D^{\lambda}$ by [F1] and lies in $B$ by hypothesis, the decomposition matrix of $B$ is the $1	imes1$ matrix with entry $d_{\lambda\lambda}=[S^{\lambda}_k:D^{\lambda}]=1$, by the exact diagonal multiplicity in [F4]. A simple head alone would not establish multiplicity one.

The Cartan matrix and the projective cover. By [F5] applied to the block $B$ the Cartan matrix of $B$ is $C_B=D_B^{\mathsf T}D_B=(1)$, so the projective cover $P^{\lambda}$ of $D^{\lambda}$ has $D^{\lambda}$ as its only composition factor, with multiplicity one. A nonzero module of length one is simple, so $P^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda}$: the block $B$ has a projective simple module.

Defect zero and the matrix algebra. By step 2.1 the projective indecomposable $P^{\lambda}$ equals the simple $D^{\lambda}$, and it is the unique projective indecomposable of $B$ because the simple modules of $B$ are in bijection with its projective indecomposables; so $D^{\lambda}$ is both the unique simple and the unique projective indecomposable of $B$. Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a
$\beta$-set for $\lambda$, so that $P(X)=\lambda$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Write $H_i(\lambda)$ for
the set of hook lengths in row $i$ of $[\lambda]$: thus $h\in H_i(\lambda)$
means $h=h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ for some node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$, and
$H_i(\lambda)=\emptyset$ for $i>\ell(\lambda)$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]).

(i) For every $h\ge0$ and every $i\in[m]$, $h\in H_i(\lambda)$ if and only if
$h\le h_i$ and $h_i-h\notin X$. Equivalently, the hooks of $\lambda$
correspond bijectively to the **bead-gap pairs** $(b,g)$ with $b\in X$,
$g\notin X$ and $0\le g<b$; the hook $H_{i,j}(\lambda)$ corresponds to
$$(b,g)=\bigl(h_i,\;h_i-h_{i,j}(\lambda)\bigr),$$
and then $|H_{i,j}(\lambda)|=b-g$.

(ii) Fix a node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$ and let $(b,g)$ be its bead-gap pair as in
(i). Then
$$X':=(X\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$$
is again a $\beta$-set, now for the partition $\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}$
obtained from $\lambda$ by removing the removable border strip $R_{i,j}$ that
corresponds to the hook of $(i,j)$, of size $h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ and height
$\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]); in terms of parts, with
$b_0:=\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$,
$$\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}=\bigl(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{i-1},\,\lambda_{i+1}-1,\dots,\lambda_{i+b_0}-1,\,j-1,\,\lambda_{i+b_0+1},\dots\bigr),$$
so that $|\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}|=n-h_{i,j}(\lambda)$. Finally $X'$ is
obtained from the configuration $A_X$ by moving the bead from position $b$ to
the gap $g$.

(iii) In particular $e\mid h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ if and only if $b\equiv g\pmod e$,
that is, if and only if the bead $b$ and the gap $g$ lie on the same runner of
the $e$-abacus; then $g=b-e\cdot(h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e)$ and the move in (ii) is
the slide of the bead $b$ up $h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e$ rows on its own runner. A
hook of length $e$ in row $i$ of $\lambda$ exists if and only if $h_i\ge e$
and $h_i-e\notin X$; Thus $\lambda$ has a hook of length $e$ if and only if some bead of $X$ has a gap
in the position $e$ labels above it on its own runner.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. Let $H(x)$ be the hook of $x$,
with arm length $a(x)=\lambda_i-j$, leg length $\ell(x)=\lambda'_j-i$ and hook
length $h(x)=a(x)+\ell(x)+1$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); its two endpoints are the last node
$(i,\lambda_i)$ of its arm and the last node $(\lambda'_j,j)$ of its leg. Let
$\xi(x)$ be the unique edge-connected set of nodes of $[\lambda]$ with
endpoints $(i,\lambda_i)$ and $(\lambda'_j,j)$ that lies in the rim of
$[\lambda]$, i.e. consists of nodes $(p,q)$ with $(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Then:

1. $\xi(x)$ is a removable border strip of $\lambda$ of size $h(x)$ and height
   $\ell(x)$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
   $[\lambda]\setminus\xi(x)$ is a Young diagram, so $\lambda\setminus\xi(x)$ is
   a partition of $n-h(x)$;
2. every removable border strip of $\lambda$ equals $\xi(x)$ for exactly one
   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes
   of $[\lambda]$ onto the removable border strips of $\lambda$.

Consequently the sizes of the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly
the hook lengths of $\lambda$, the height of $\xi(x)$ is the leg length
$\ell(x)$, and $x$ is removable as a node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) if and only if $\xi(x)$
has size $1$. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Fix a $\beta$-set $X$ of a partition $\mu$ and write its elements as $h_1>\cdots>h_m$. By [F1] the hooks of length $e$ of $\mu$ correspond bijectively to the beads $b=h_i$ with $h_i\ge e$ and $h_i-e\notin X$, the correspondence sending such a bead to the rim strip $R_{i,j}(\mu)$ attached to the node with $h_{i,j}(\mu)=e$, and removal of that strip replaces $X$ by $X'=(X\setminus\{h_i\})\cup\{h_i-e\}$, a $\beta$-set for $\mu\setminus R_{i,j}(\mu)$ of the same size $m$. In particular $\mu$ has no hook of length $e$ exactly when no bead of $X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own runner.

Compute the shift directly. For $Y=X+1$, its runner sets are $Y^{(e)}_0=(X^{(e)}_{e-1})+1$ and $Y^{(e)}_i=X^{(e)}_{i-1}$ for $1\le i<e$: the last runner wraps to runner $0$ one row lower, and the shift adds the bead at $0$. Its counts are $(c_{e-1}+1,c_0,\ldots,c_{e-2})$. Packing with these counts gives $Y^{(e)}=(X^{(e)})+1$, so $P(Y^{(e)})=P(X^{(e)})$ by [F3]. Iteration proves core independence for all beta-sets of $\lambda$. After $e$ shifts, every runner row-label set has undergone one beta-set shift by $1$, so its partition is unchanged. Normalised beta-sets differ by a multiple of $e$, proving independence of the ordered quotient and its total size.

Call a bead of $X$ *movable* when the position $e$ labels above it on its runner is a gap, so that by step 1.1 the movable beads are exactly the hooks of length $e$ of $\mu$; moving a bead up one row replaces $X$ by a $\beta$-set of $\mu$ minus that hook, and the counts $|X^{(e)}_i|$ of beads on each runner are unchanged. A configuration is top-packed precisely when it has no movable bead: a top-packed runner carries beads in the rows $0,1,\dots,c_i-1$, so the row above a bead is a bead again (and row $0$ has no row above it), while if some runner is not top-packed there are a gap in row $g$ and a bead in a row $a>g$ on that runner; choosing $a$ minimal among the bead rows larger than $g$, the row $a-1$ is a gap, so the bead in row $a$ is movable.

Every sequence of moves of steps 1.1 and 2.1 is finite: the quantity $\Phi:=\sum_{i}\sum_{a\in X^{(e)}_i}a$ is the total of the row labels of all beads, and each move replaces a bead's row label $a$ by $a-1$, so $\Phi$ decreases by exactly $1$ and is a nonnegative integer. A sequence is maximal exactly when it stops at a configuration with no movable bead, that is, by step 2.1, exactly when it stops at the top-packed configuration of the counts $(c_i)$; and that configuration is unique, since a runner with $c_i$ beads has exactly one top-packed state, the rows $0,\dots,c_i-1$. Hence every maximal sequence of moves starting from $X$ ends at the same configuration, namely $X^{(e)}$, and therefore at the same terminal partition $P(X^{(e)})$.

By step 1.2 the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ does not depend on the chosen $\beta$-set $X$, so $C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)})$ is well-defined; by step 3.1 it is the common terminal partition of all maximal sequences of e-hook removals, and by step 2.1 a terminal configuration is top-packed, hence carries no movable bead, hence its partition has no hook of length $e$ by step 1.1; thus $C_e(\lambda)$ is an $e$-core. Every strip removed along such a sequence corresponds to a node hook of length exactly $e$ and so has size $e$ by [F4]. This proves all the asserted properties.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a
$\beta$-set for $\lambda$, so that $P(X)=\lambda$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Write $H_i(\lambda)$ for
the set of hook lengths in row $i$ of $[\lambda]$: thus $h\in H_i(\lambda)$
means $h=h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ for some node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$, and
$H_i(\lambda)=\emptyset$ for $i>\ell(\lambda)$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]).

(i) For every $h\ge0$ and every $i\in[m]$, $h\in H_i(\lambda)$ if and only if
$h\le h_i$ and $h_i-h\notin X$. Equivalently, the hooks of $\lambda$
correspond bijectively to the **bead-gap pairs** $(b,g)$ with $b\in X$,
$g\notin X$ and $0\le g<b$; the hook $H_{i,j}(\lambda)$ corresponds to
$$(b,g)=\bigl(h_i,\;h_i-h_{i,j}(\lambda)\bigr),$$
and then $|H_{i,j}(\lambda)|=b-g$.

(ii) Fix a node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$ and let $(b,g)$ be its bead-gap pair as in
(i). Then
$$X':=(X\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$$
is again a $\beta$-set, now for the partition $\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}$
obtained from $\lambda$ by removing the removable border strip $R_{i,j}$ that
corresponds to the hook of $(i,j)$, of size $h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ and height
$\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]); in terms of parts, with
$b_0:=\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$,
$$\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}=\bigl(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{i-1},\,\lambda_{i+1}-1,\dots,\lambda_{i+b_0}-1,\,j-1,\,\lambda_{i+b_0+1},\dots\bigr),$$
so that $|\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}|=n-h_{i,j}(\lambda)$. Finally $X'$ is
obtained from the configuration $A_X$ by moving the bead from position $b$ to
the gap $g$.

(iii) In particular $e\mid h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ if and only if $b\equiv g\pmod e$,
that is, if and only if the bead $b$ and the gap $g$ lie on the same runner of
the $e$-abacus; then $g=b-e\cdot(h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e)$ and the move in (ii) is
the slide of the bead $b$ up $h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e$ rows on its own runner. A
hook of length $e$ in row $i$ of $\lambda$ exists if and only if $h_i\ge e$
and $h_i-e\notin X$; Thus $\lambda$ has a hook of length $e$ if and only if some bead of $X$ has a gap
in the position $e$ labels above it on its own runner.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column

A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of

derivations.claim: Write a hook $H=H_{i,j}(\lambda)$ of $e$-divisible length in its bead-gap form $(b,g)$ with $b\in X$, $g\notin X$, $0\le g<b$ and $h:=|H|=b-g$. By $e\mid h$ we have $b\equiv g\pmod e$; write the common residue as $s\in\{0,\dots,e-1\}$ and $$b=b'e+s,\qquad g=g'e+s,\qquad b'=\frac{b-s}{e}>g'=\frac{g-s}{e}\ge0.$$ The bead $b$ is a bead of $X$ on runner $s$ and the gap $g$ is a gap of $X$ on runner $s$.

Applying step 1.1 conversely, a bead $b'\in X^{(e)}_s$ and a gap $g'\notin X^{(e)}_s$ with $0\le g'<b'$ give the bead-gap pair $(b,g)=(b'e+s,g'e+s)$ of $X$ with $e\mid(b-g)$ and $b-g=e(b'-g')$. Hence $f(H):=$ the hook of $\lambda^{(s)}$ attached to the bead-gap pair $(b',g')$ of the $\beta$-set $X^{(e)}_s$ is well defined, and $f$ is bijective onto the hooks of $\bigsqcup_i\lambda^{(i)}$ because both sides are in bijection with the bead-gap pairs of $X$ whose two positions share a runner, respectively with the union over $s$ of the bead-gap pairs of $X^{(e)}_s$; the length identity is $|H|=b-g=e(b'-g')=e|f(H)|$.

For the removal identity, let $X'=(X\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$ be the $\beta$-set of $\lambda\setminus H$ from [F1], again of size $m$ and hence normalised by [F3]. Because $b$ and $g$ lie on runner $s$, the beads of $X'$ on a runner $t\ne s$ are exactly the beads of $X$ on runner $t$, and the beads on runner $s$ have row labels $(X^{(e)}_s\setminus\{b'\})\cup\{g'\}$. Consequently, computing the quotient from the normalised sets by [F2], $$\lambda'^{(t)}=P\bigl((X')^{(e)}_t\bigr)=\lambda^{(t)}\ (t\ne s),\qquad \lambda'^{(s)}=P\bigl((X^{(e)}_s\setminus\{b'\})\cup\{g'\}\bigr),$$ and the last partition is $\lambda^{(s)}$ with its hook $f(H)$ removed, by [F1] applied to the $\beta$-set $X^{(e)}_s$ of $\lambda^{(s)}$. This is exactly the assertion $Q_e(\lambda\setminus H)=Q_e(\lambda)\setminus f(H)$.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 together exhibit the required bijection $f$ with the length and removal identities, and the description of $f$ on the abacus is the rescaling of step 1.1 followed by the bead-gap dictionary of the runner in step 2.1.

This fixes the actual module-and-form normalization used by the corner and weight-Gram calculations (Mathas (4.13), with Corollary 4.12 and Theorem 4.14). No quantum factorial is inverted in this definition.

**Weight idempotents and weight spaces.** For each composition $

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ a cellular $R$-algebra with cellular basis
$(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$
there is a unique $R$-bilinear form
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:C^{\lambda}\times C^{\lambda}\longrightarrow R$$
with
$$c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in T(\lambda)$; in particular the right hand side is
independent of $u$ and $v$, and $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$
depends only on $s,t$. This form is (i) symmetric,
$\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$; (ii) associative,
$\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $a\in A$,
where $i(a)y$ denotes the right action $y\,i(a)$ of $i(a)$ on $y$, i.e. the
left action $a\cdot y:=y\,i(a)$; (iii) characterised by
$x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_v$ for
$x\in C^{\lambda}$; and (iv) its radical
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}:=\{x\in C^{\lambda}:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\text{ for all }y\in C^{\lambda}\}$
is an $A$-submodule of $C^{\lambda}$, namely the kernel of
$x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$ the residue field, and let $\hat q\in R^{	imes}$ satisfy $[n]!_{\hat q}
e0$ in $R$; put $q:=\hat q+\pi R\in F^{	imes}$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl module of the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)=S(d,n)\otimes_RF$ with its Jantzen filtration $W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ with respect to $(R,\pi)$ ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

1. (**Jantzen sum formula**) In the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $S_F(d,n)$-modules, $$\sum_{i>0} igl[W^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr],$$ where $ eta= eta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$, $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. 2. (**q-Schaper, $d\ge n$**) If $d\ge n$ and $\Pi$ denotes the Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], then applying $\Pi$ to (1) gives the corresponding identity for the Hecke Specht modules in the source's normalisation, that is, for the Murphy cell modules $\Pi(W^{\lambda}_F)=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ of [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]] (the Dipper-James form is obtained by conjugating partitions and applying the same $	heta$ pullback to every Hecke module), $$\sum_{i>0} igl[S^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr]$$ in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with the virtual Specht symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The formula is a positive filtration-sum identity expressed in a signed Weyl/Specht basis. A single nonzero signed Weyl coefficient does not force the corresponding labelled simple factor: the entire right side must first be expanded and cancelled in simple classes. For a Weyl module and an off-head label $
u$, the resulting multiplicity of $L^
u$ is an upper bound for $[W^\lambda:L^
u]$, and is positive exactly when that factor occurs in the radical. This does not give a general closed algorithm for decomposition numbers.

Fix a beta length $L\ge1$. For a partition $
u$ with at most $L$ columns (that is, $
u_1\le L$), put $$ eta_i(
u)=
u'_i+L-i\qquad(1\le i\le L).$$ Its beta numbers are strictly decreasing nonnegative integers. Conversely, from any strictly decreasing nonnegative sequence $b$ recover the unique partition with conjugate parts $
u'_i=b_i-L+i$, of degree $|
u|=\sum_i b_i-L(L-1)/2$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

For arbitrary $b\in\mathbb Z^L$, first set all its alternating symbols to zero if it has repeated entries or a negative entry. Otherwise there is a unique sorting permutation $w$ taking it to decreasing order; let $
u$ be the recovered partition and let $\epsilon(b)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$. Uniqueness of the sorting permutation is claimed only in this distinct-entry case. In the fixed degree-$r$ Grothendieck groups define $$[W^b]_{d,r}:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[W^
u],&|
u|=r	ext{ and } \ell(
u)\le d,\0,&	ext{otherwise},\end{cases} \qquad [S^b]_r:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[S_{\mathrm M}^
u],&|
u|=r,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$ The notation $[\Delta^b]$ is synonymous with $[W^b]_{d,r}$ when $d,r$ are fixed. The ordinary Dipper-James translation conjugates every partition label and pulls every compared module back by the same $	heta$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

For a composition $\mu$ define the signed semistandard number directly by $$d_\mu(b):= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)|T_0(
u,\mu)|,&b	ext{ has distinct nonnegative entries and }|
u|=|\mu|,\0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ Here the tableau alphabet is the length of $\mu$; a shape with too many rows automatically has no such tableau ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]). This function is alternating in the beta entries. It also obeys the branching identity $$d_\mu(b)=\sum_{\substack{C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}\|C|=z}}  d_{ ar\mu}(b-\mathbf1_C),$$ where $z$ is the last nonzero part of $\mu$ and $ ar\mu$ deletes that part. The selected entries are **decreased by one**, not replaced by $-1$. For a decreasing beta sequence this is the deletion of the largest semistandard entries: they occupy a horizontal strip, at most one box in each selected column. Sorting extends the identity to distinct arbitrary sequences; if entries repeat, terms selecting just one of the equal entries cancel in pairs, while terms selecting both or neither vanish. Negative entries remain negative after decrementing. Thus the identity also holds in all zero-symbol cases. At $\mu=0$ its value is the sorting sign for a permutation of $(L-1,\ldots,0)$ and is zero otherwise, so the recursion terminates without another unproved extension rule.

In the formulas of this page take $L=r$ when $r>0$. A nonzero degree-$r$ partition has width at most $r$, so this length suffices; the Weyl cutoff $\ell(
u)\le d$ is retained even when $d<r$. A balanced displacement $+h\mathbf e_b-h\mathbf e_c$ preserves total degree. An unbalanced change is not silently treated as a class in the same fixed-degree group. The empty degree is handled by the empty beta sequence and unit symbol. No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S=S(d,n)$ be the
$q$-Schur algebra over $F$ with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$ for
$\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Let $M$ be a finite
dimensional right $S$-module all of whose composition factors lie in a single
block $B$ of $S$
([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and let integers $a_{\lambda}$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$, satisfy
$$[M]=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$$
in the Grothendieck group $G_0(S\text{-mod})$
([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]). Then
$W^{\lambda}$ lies in $B$ whenever $a_{\lambda}\ne0$. In particular no nonzero
virtual combination of Weyl classes all of whose terms lie outside $B$ can
equal the class of a module in $B$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then
$J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.

Let $R$ be a nonzero unital ring. Then $R$ is semisimple if and only if $$R\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i)$$ for positive integers $r,n_i$ and division rings $D_i$. See [[thm-endomorphism-ring-of-the-left-regular-module-is-opposite]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

derivations.claim: Lift and valuation. Use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ with $\hat q=X$ and uniformizer $X-q$. The element $X$ is a unit since $q\ne0$, and every polynomial $[m]_X=1+X+\cdots+X^{m-1}$ is nonzero, so the generic factorial is nonzero. For $n=0$, $S_F(d,0)=F$, with its one empty-label module, so all assertions hold directly; hence assume $n>0$. Its valuation $v(m)$ is positive exactly when $[m]_q=0$, equivalently $e\mid m$ for finite $e$; for $e=\infty$ all valuations vanish. In characteristic $p$ the positive valuation may exceed1, which causes no difficulty below.

Block support and Jantzen edges. A finite-dimensional module with simple head is indecomposable: every nonzero summand has nonzero head, so two summands would make the head nonsimple. Thus $W^{\lambda}$ has just one nonzero block summand, and every Jantzen submodule is supported in that block. By [F4], any nonzero accumulated coefficient $J_{\lambda\mu}$ of $[W^{\mu}]$ in [F2] puts $W^{\lambda},W^{\mu}$ in the same block. This uses the sum of submodule classes, without identifying it with the radical class.

Balanced terms preserve the core and descend in dominance. Put $s=h_{ab}$ and $t=h_{ac}$, so $s-t=\beta_b-\beta_c$. If a hook coefficient is nonzero, at least one of $s,t$ is divisible by $e$. If $e\mid t$, the shifted bead residues are unchanged. Otherwise $e\mid s$, so $t\equiv\beta_c-\beta_b\pmod e$ and the two shifted residues exchange. Thus every surviving symbol has the same runner counts and core as $\lambda$. Moreover replacing the two conjugate beta entries $u>v$ by $u+t,v-t$ strictly increases conjugate majorization; the sorted target therefore strictly decreases original dominance. Accumulating equal target labels preserves both conclusions.

No outgoing edge implies a binary row condition. Suppose every accumulated outgoing coefficient from $\mu$ is zero. For row $i$, put $g_i=N+i-1-\mu_i$, a gap in its conjugate beta set; its row hooks are exactly $\beta_j-g_i>0$. If that row contained a divisible hook $s$ and a nondivisible hook $t$, repeatedly replace $t$ by $s+t$ while their sum is another row hook. This finite climb ends with $s+t$ absent from the hook set. The balanced term for the nodes of hook lengths $s,t$ then has lower shifted bead $g_i$, which is a gap, and upper shifted bead $g_i+s+t$, which is absent from the beta set. Its symbol survives and its coefficient is $\pm v(s)\ne0$. There is no cancellation: any surviving balanced term replaces two lost values by a new value larger than both and a new value smaller than both, so those four values determine the pair and its row gap uniquely; the gaps $g_i$ strictly increase with $i$. This contradicts the zero accumulated coefficient. Therefore each row has either all hook lengths divisible by $e$ or none; call this the binary row condition.

Vertical core removal under the binary row condition. A removable $e$-hook has hook length $e$ at its defining node. Every hook in that row is then divisible, so its last-column hook, a positive multiple of $e$ no larger than $e$, equals $e$. Hook lengths strictly decrease across the row, forcing the defining node to be at the row end: the strip is vertical on $e$ equal-length rows $i,\ldots,i+e-1$ in column $j$. Removing it decreases that column height by $e$. In unaffected rows hook divisibility is unchanged. For an affected row $i+t$, hooks in the retained columns were all congruent to $-t$ modulo $e$, because row $i$ had all hooks divisible and those rows had equal length. Their new hook lengths are all congruent to $-t-1$, so the binary row condition persists. Induction shows every core-removal strip is vertical.

The Cartan graph locally. Choose a complete orthogonal primitive idempotent system of $S$, with one representative $f_\mu$ for each simple label and repeated representatives as necessary. By [F5] and the absolute simplicity in [F1], the semisimple quotient is a product of full matrix rings over $F$. Lift its matrix diagonal idempotents: the radical is nilpotent and the iteration $u\mapsto u+(1-2u)(u^2-u)$ changes an error $a=u^2-u$ to $-3a^2+4a^3$, so finite iteration lifts an idempotent; successively working in complementary corners lifts an orthogonal system. Absolute simplicity gives $\dim L^{\lambda}f_\mu=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, hence exact multiplication by $f_\mu$ gives $\dim W^{\lambda}f_\mu=d_{\lambda\mu}$. The successive cellular ideal bimodules are the contragredient cell module tensor the right cell module. Apply the exact projection $f_\mu(-)f_
u$ and add their dimensions; [F1]'s duality fixes the simple labels, giving $\dim f_\mu Sf_
u=\sum_\lambda d_{\lambda\mu}d_{\lambda
u}$. This is the Cartan entry of the primitive projective $f_\mu S$. A disconnected graph on the full primitive idempotent system, with edges whenever either mixed corner is nonzero, yields central idempotents by summing each component: all mixed corners vanish in both directions. Conversely a central block idempotent forbids mixed corners. Thus simple labels in one block are joined by pairs sharing a Weyl factor, and step 3.1 proves that labels in the same block have the same core.

The minimum label and the bridge shapes. Assume $e<\infty$. Fix core $\gamma$ and weight $w$, with $l=\ell(\gamma)$, and set $ho=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_l,1^{ew})$. It has core $\gamma$ by removing its bottom vertical $e$-strips, and is dominance-minimal in the class: every same-core partition contains $\gamma$ as a diagram, and appending all additional boxes as rows of size1 minimizes each dominance partial sum. Let $\mu
eho$ satisfy the binary row condition. Choose the first row $i$ with divisible hooks and put $j=\mu_i$, $h=h^{\mu}_{ij}=\mu'_j-i+1$, a positive multiple of $e$. If $j=1$, every divisible hook is in column1, so step 3.2 would give $\mu=ho$; thus $j>1$. Remove the vertical $h$-strip, obtaining $\sigma$, then add $h$ boxes horizontally to its first row to get $
u$, and vertically to its first column to get $\eta$. All have the same core, since $h$ is a multiple of $e$; $
u$ dominates $\mu,\eta$, and $\eta$ is strictly below $\mu$ because the removed nodes are moved into new bottom rows.

Connectivity and sufficiency. Induct upwards from $\rho$ in the finite dominance poset. For $\mu\ne\rho$, if an outgoing coefficient $J_{\mu\tau}$ is nonzero, then $\tau$ is strictly below $\mu$ in the same core class by step 2.1, so induction connects $\tau$, and hence $\mu$, to $\rho$. If no outgoing coefficient exists, steps 2.2, 3.2, 4.2 and 5.1 connect $\mu$ to $\nu$ and then $\eta$, with $\eta$ strictly below $\mu$, and induction again connects it to $\rho$. Every such edge is a same-block implication by step 1.2. Thus every pair of labels of the same core lies in the same block. Together with step 4.1 this proves the equivalence.

Parameterization and infinite characteristic. Every simple is the head of a Weyl module, so every block has a partition label. The core sizes are $n-ew$, and each admissible core occurs via the partition $\rho$ of step 4.2; step 6.1 therefore gives the stated indexing. If $e=\infty$, all coefficients vanish by step 1.1, so positivity forces every first Jantzen submodule, hence every radical, to vanish. All Weyl modules are simple; their decomposition matrix is the identity. Step 4.1 then gives identity Cartan matrix, so every primitive projective is simple and $S$ is semisimple, with each partition its own block and core. This proves all assertions.

risk_review.notes: Checked all eleven current proof steps and the balanced Jantzen, alternating beta, Weyl/simple-head and finite-block supplier interfaces. The positive Jantzen sum is a sum of submodules, never identified wholesale with the radical. Balanced shifts preserve runner residues and strict dominance. The no-outgoing-edge argument isolates a unique surviving two-lost/two-gained bead term, forcing the binary row condition. Vertical removal preserves that condition; bridge partitions connect each exceptional label to a strictly lower same-core label via nonzero accumulated coefficients. The finite Cartan graph proves necessity, the dominance-minimum induction proves sufficiency. Degree zero is scalar, infinite characteristic has zero valuations and identity Cartan, and d>=n is retained.
